name: Kamoro
confidence_why: Voorhoeve (1975) reports that Drabbe's 1953 grammar marks stress on individual Kamoro words but gives no placement rule, Drabbe's grammar and Boelaars's 1950 recension of it are not accessible, and none of the other works read (Ray 1912, Rawling 1913, Voorhoeve 1968, 1980, 2005, Usher 2024) says anything about Kamoro stress, so no placement or system type can be defended.
catalog_citation: Pawley, Andrew & Harald Hammarström. 2018. The Trans New Guinea family. In Bill Palmer (ed.), The Languages and Linguistics of the New Guinea Area: A Comprehensive Guide (The World of Linguistics 4), 21-195. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. Section 2.4.3 'Prosody', pp. 88-89.
catalog_locator: section 2.4.3 'Prosody', pp. 88 and 89; Kamoro listed as 'Kamoro [kgq] 8,000 grammar: Drabbe 1953' in section 2.3.1.3 Asmat-Kamoro, p. 36
catalog_quote: [p. 88] Similarly, most members of the Asmat-Kamoro group lack tonal prosody but Kamoro and Citak Asmat are tonal and these are in contact with cordilleran languages. [...] [p. 89] Ross maps the distribution of tonal types in TNG languages of West Papua as follows. In the far west word-tone or syllable-tone systems occur in certain Paniai Lakes languages (Wolani and Moni) and in the disputed TNG isolate Uhunduni. Ekari (Paniai Lakes), Kamoro (Asmat-Kamoro) and the Western Dani languages have pitch-accent prosody.

new_statements.quote: Kamoro has a very simple sound system. It has only three stops, p, t, k [k, g, x] or ʔ (Kamora dialect); two nasals m [m, mb], n [n, nd]; one vibrant r; two semi-vowels, w, and y; and five, perhaps six, vowel phonemes [...]. Stress is indicated by Drabbe on individual words, but no rules of stress placement are given.
new_statements.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1975. Central and Western Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1, 345-460. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics C-38.
new_statements.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (116 pp., ANU Open Research scan of Pacific Linguistics C-38) and its page extract. PDF page 26 = printed p. 370, section 2.6.2.2.6.1.2 'Kamoro'. The text (letter-spaced scanned) reads, after space-stripping: 'Kamoro has a very simple sound system. It has only three stops, p, t, k [k, g, x] or ? (Kamora dialect); two nasals m [m, mb], n [n, nd]; one vibrant r; two semi-vowels, w, and y; and five, perhaps six, vowel phonemes: i, e [e..], a, o [o..], u, (a). Stress is indicated by Drabbe on individual words, but no rules of stress placement are given.' The reported quote matches this verbatim; its [..] is a marked ellipsis of the vowel list and it normalises the scanned '?' to the glot…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is available: the only full description (Drabbe 1953, Tarya dialect) marks stress word by word and, according to Voorhoeve's survey, states no rule for where it falls. The Drabbe forms relayed by Usher show stress on the first syllable in some words (ˈkimiri, ˈpikiri, ˈupuka) and on a later syllable in others (kaˈta, paˈjakɔ, muruˈkua), so a simple fixed-position rule is not evident from the data either.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source says explicitly that no rules are given.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (stress marked on individual words in a grammar's citation forms); dialect described is Tarya (Opa River). Kamoro has 6-7 dialects and Usher/Wikipedia note it may be more than one language.
new_statements.identity_note: All modern descriptions rest on Drabbe 1953, which describes the Tarya (Tarjà) dialect of the Opa River; Kamoro (kamo1255, language-level) has six plains dialects (Western, Tarya, Middle, Kamora, Wania, Mukumuga) plus an Etna Bay/Yamur Lake variety (Nanesa, Peckham 1991), and Usher notes it may be several languages. No dialect-level glottocodes located.

tone_statements.citation: Donohue, Mark. 1997. Tone systems in New Guinea. Linguistic Typology 1(3): 347-386. doi:10.1515/lity.1997.1.3.347
tone_statements.quote: [K]amoro (Drabbe 1953; Donohue 1993) shows a very similar system, [thou]gh Drabbe explicitly mentions that Kamoro allows more than one [accen]t per word, if the word is composed of several morphemes, showing [that in] this language at least the domain of the pitch accent is the [morph]eme, not the word ... Examples of this so[rt of] system are Una, Kamoro, Arigibi Kiwai, Isirawa, Marind, Kaure, [and] possibly Ekari.
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Kamoro has a Kiwai-like pitch accent system (at least one unaccented syllable per word) except that a polymorphemic word can carry one accent per morpheme. This is the primary statement behind the entry's secondhand 'pitch accent prosody' from Pawley & Hammarström; no forms are given.

sources.citation: Usher, Timothy (with Edgar Suter). Kamoro. New Guinea World, newguineaworld.linguistik.uzh.ch, page last modified 2024-06-25 (phonology of Tarya Kamoro after Drabbe 1953: 4-6; dialect data from Drabbe 1953: 80-86, 96-104 and Peckham 1991).
sources.note: Phonology section says nothing about stress. The Tarya forms it copies from Drabbe carry stress marks that fall in different positions (e.g. ˈkimiri 'wind', ˈpikiri 'skin', ˈupuka 'man', ˈnenəkə 'heart' vs kaˈta 'evil', paˈjakɔ 'wide', atɔˈa 'big', muruˈkua 'short', aˈkajta 'thus'), i.e. no single position rule is visible in the data as relayed.

tone.quote: 2) Fonem-fonem Suprasegmental /e/ – /ee/ Kontras bunyi depan-tengah pendek dan panjang [...] Masalah suprasegmental dalam bahasa Kamoro, tidak saja diketahui adanya fonem-fonem vokal panjang, tetapi terdapat pula perihal glotal yang sebenarnya merupakan variasi bunyi dari fonem /k/. [...] [Simpulan:] Dalam ragam bahasa ini hanya terdapat suku kata terbuka, sehingga hanya ada dua jenis pola suku kata, yakni V dan KV. Tekanan jatuh pada suku kata akhir.
tone.locator: p. 227, Hasil dan Pembahasan, '2 Fonem-fonem Suprasegmental'; p. 233, 'Simpulan' (same stress sentence also in the abstract, p. 224)
tone.translation: 2) Suprasegmental phonemes: /e/ - /ee/ contrast of short and long front-mid sounds [...] As regards suprasegmentals in Kamoro, not only are long vowel phonemes known to exist, there is also the matter of the glottal stop, which is really a sound variant of the phoneme /k/. [...] [Conclusion:] In this variety there are only open syllables, so there are only two syllable patterns, V and CV. Stress falls on the final syllable.
